leads.name: Bruine beuk, Hortus entrance (LRMB 1679547)
leads.why: Felled. The register's own historie note ends 'Gevolgd door het rooien van de boom, november 1987': planted 1816, giant polypore infection from 1984, removed November 1987. The entry survives in the register as a historical record, not as a standing tree. Never publish.

leads.name: Japanse Notenboom / Ginkgo, Hortus (LRMB 1679548)
leads.why: Already published as lei_002, The Ginkgo of the Hortus. Same tree: 1785, female branch grafted 1935, glasshouse complex built around it in 1938. The register's surveyed coordinate has been applied to lei_002 and its pin upgraded to confirmed.

leads.name: Treurbeuk, Hortus (LRMB 1690081)
leads.why: Already published as lei_003, The Weeping Beech of the Hortus. Same tree: planted around 1840, successor obtained in 1982 from the Amsterdam Floriade. The register's surveyed coordinate has been applied to lei_003 and its pin upgraded to confirmed.

leads.name: De bruine beuk van de Groenesteeg (LRMB 1690124)
leads.why: Already published as lei_006, The Groenesteeg Beech. Same tree: the thickest beech in South Holland, in the middle of Groenesteeg cemetery. It slipped the 50m dedupe filter because our published pin was approximate and 62m off. The register's surveyed coordinate has been applied to lei_006 and its pin upgraded to confirmed.

leads.name: The Fern-leaved Beech of the Nut Field
leads.age_estimate: planted 1800-1850, and 1818 by the register's own note, so between 175 and 225 years

location.address: Hortus Botanicus Leiden, along the path on the Notenveld

leads.story: The oldest fern-leaved beech in the Netherlands is also one of the three thickest, and it has had two centuries of elbow room to get that way. The register puts it in the ground in 1818, while the Hortus was growing and being relaid in the English landscape style, out on the open patch the garden calls the Notenveld, the nut field, among trees kept here for what they drop. Nothing crowds it, so it grew the way a beech grows when nothing is competing for the light: outward rather than upward, into one enormous low dome. Fern-leaved beech is a form of the ordinary European beech whose leaves are cut into narrow lobes, fine enough that from a few metres away the crown reads as feathered rather than leafed. Up close the trunk does something else entirely. It is vaulted and swollen, bulging in some places and open in others, the sort of surface people put a hand on without quite deciding to. Come in spring and the ground competes for attention: stinzenplanten, the old Dutch estate bulbs that naturalise under mature trees, come up in sheets underneath before the beech leafs out and takes the light back. The formal planting band on the register runs 1800 to 1850, so the age is between 175 and 225 years.
leads.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
leads.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station

best_time.label: April, when the stinzen bulbs flower underneath and the fern-cut leaves open

leads.pulled_from_city: Published until 2026-08-23. Ten of Leiden's fourteen trees stood inside the Hortus behind a 14 euro ticket, which is a garden list wearing a city's name. These five are the 19th-century collection specimens with no photograph; the four 18th-century veterans stayed, because a 310-year tulip tree in the country's oldest botanical garden is worth the ticket. Removed on reach and on padding, never on truth: every fact was verified.

leads.name: The Grafted Ash of the Hortus
leads.story: This ash has spent two hundred years slowly swallowing its own graft. It was planted in 1818 and grafted, probably at around two metres up the stem, where the join left the swelling that grafts always leave. The Dutch word for that bulge is slobbertrui, a baggy jumper, and on this tree it has travelled downward. The register records the swelling sinking further down the trunk decade by decade, until today it sits a few decimetres above the soil on one side and less than a decimetre on the other. Partly because of all that accumulated tissue, the register calls it the thickest narrow-leaved ash in the country. Fraxinus angustifolia comes from southern Europe and North Africa, drier and warmer country than a botanical garden in the Dutch coastal plain, and it wears the family look in a slimmer cut: leaflets narrower and more sharply pointed than the common ash standing beside every ditch in the province. Its recorded planting band runs 1810 to 1820, which puts it a little past two hundred years old. The garden's fern-leaved beech went into the ground the same year. Ash dieback has been working through Europe's ash population for two decades now, killing young and old alike, which makes a healthy veteran of this size worth the detour on its own.

leads.name: Bruine beuk, Herenhuis Boisotkade (LRMB 1697142)
leads.why: 2026-09-07 verify pass. Register's own field says visitable: nee (not visitable) and place is 'Garenmarkt 9, Leiden', a private townhouse (herenhuis). Somebody's home; never publish per hard rule 10.

leads.name: 9 Zilveresdoorns Werfpark (LRMB 1690140)
leads.why: 2026-09-07 verify pass. Register counts n_trees: 9, planted 1886 in a semicircle behind the Van der Werff statue. Not a single collectible point: nine trees in a row/arc is an avenue-like planting, no one obvious place to stand at ONE tree, same shape as the Barcelona plane-avenue precedent that failed this test. Confirmed by openbomenkaart.org's historical page for the park, which also describes them only as a group ('de negen zilveresdoorns... in een halve cirkel achter het beeld').

leads.name: Leopoldii esdoorn Van der Werfpark (LRMB 1690137) and Bontbladige esdoorn Van der Werfpark (LRMB 1693443)
leads.why: 2026-09-07 verify pass. Two register entries only 33m apart, both near the Van der Werff statue, both almost certainly the same ornamental cultivar (Bontbladige esdoorn is the common Dutch name for Acer pseudoplatanus 'Leopoldii', confirmed via nursery sources): 1690137 is 'bij standbeeld', 1693443 is noted '25 meter vanaf het standbeeld in oostelijke richting', which reads as two distinct nearby specimens rather than one duplicated record, but this pass ran out of time to find a tree-specific second source (register only) or to settle whether publishing both would read as near-duplicate pages. Worth a closer look: pick the stronger-sited one and fold the other into its story, or find independent corroboration for both.

leads.name: Moerascypres Van der Werfpark (LRMB 1690138)
leads.why: 2026-09-07 verify pass. Register counts n_trees: 3, planted 1886, 'nabij standbeeld' (near the statue), visually striking bald cypresses at the water's edge. No tree-specific second source found this pass beyond the register and openbomenkaart's generic park history page (which doesn't name the cypresses specifically). Also an ensemble-of-3 question like the silver maples, though three bald cypresses at one water's-edge spot could plausibly pass the compact-ensemble test where the maple row does not; worth a closer look with more time.

leads.name: Beuk Burcht Leiden (LRMB 1679552)
leads.why: 2026-09-07 verify pass. Register counts n_trees: 2, 'Binnen De Burcht', planted 1900-1910, history 'nog geen historische gegevens bekend' (no historical data yet known). absolutefacts.nl's independent Burcht page says exactly 'twee beuken en een iep' (two beeches and an elm) stand inside the Burcht; the already-published lei_005 (Beets Beech, matching register 1690110 'Beetsbeuk buitenring') plus this 2-tree entry would total three beeches, one more than that source counts, so it is unclear whether this entry overlaps with lei_005's registration or is genuinely additional. Left undelivered this pass rather than guessed; the elm (LRMB 1679553) was delivered as lei_024 since it is unambiguously the one elm both sources agree on.

leads.name: Rode paardenkastanje, Buiten de Burcht (LRMB 1690111)
leads.why: 2026-09-07 verify pass. Register status field is 5 (uncommon among Leiden entries, seen on several other records including one confirmed-felled tree elsewhere in this file, though status 5 alone does not reliably mean dead across the wider register: it is common, ~28% of all 16094 entries, with only a weak correlation to felling language). No second source found this pass and not enough time to chase one; needs a dedicated look before delivering.

leads.name: Gouden Regen / Judasboom / Juttepeer cluster near Hortus entrance (LRMB area ~52.1577,4.4863-4.4866)
leads.species: mixed (Laburnum anagyroides, Cercis siliquastrum, Pyrus communis)
leads.why: 2026-09-07 verify pass. Three register candidates about 0.3km from the Hortus, not individually researched this pass: this pass deliberately prioritised FREE public-park trees (Van der Werfpark, Plantsoen, the Burcht) over the Hortus area, since Leiden already sits at roughly two-thirds paid-entry trees (8 of 12 published trees require the Hortus ticket) against CLAUDE.md's rough one-third ceiling. Worth checking whether this cluster sits on Hortus grounds (paid) or a free public street/garden before a future pass researches it.
